content: BTG1 is a protein in humans encoded by the BTG1 gene. This gene is implicated in a chromosomal translocation involving chromosomes 8 and 12, specifically at (8;12)(q24;q22), which has been observed in cases of B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia. BTG1 belongs to a family of antiproliferative genes. Its expression peaks during the G0/G1 phases of the cell cycle and decreases as cells progress through the G1 phase. Functionally, BTG1 acts as a negative regulator of cell proliferation. BTG1 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including CNOT7, CNOT8, HOXB9, and PRMT1. Clinically, recurrent mutations in the BTG1 gene have been associated with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. BTG1 plays a critical role in maintaining adult neural stem cells in a quiescent state, thereby preserving the neural stem cell pool and preventing its depletion. In the absence of BTG1, neural stem and progenitor cells initially undergo hyperproliferation but eventually lose their ability to proliferate and expand over time. Interestingly, recent studies suggest that physical exercise can fully restore the proliferative capacity of stem cells following BTG1 gene ablation. This finding indicates that the neural stem cell pool retains a hidden form of plasticity, tightly regulated by BTG1. Consequently, BTG1 may prevent the depletion of stem cells under conditions of strong neurogenic or neurodegenerative stimuli. BTG1 also plays a role in the expansion of cerebellar granule precursor cells. In mice, deletion of BTG1 leads to uncontrolled proliferation of cerebellar precursor cells during the early postnatal period. As a result, adult mice lacking BTG1 exhibit significantly larger cerebella and severe impairments in motor coordination. The closest homolog of BTG1 is BTG2, which also regulates the proliferation and differentiation of adult neural stem cells. However, the role of BTG2 appears to differ from that of BTG1, as BTG2 is likely more involved in controlling the terminal differentiation of neural stem and progenitor cells within adult neurogenic niches.
